items.stem: Which of the following statements about natural frequency, forced oscillations and resonance is a common misconception? (Revision quiz set by Hana.)
options: There is no net energy transfer along a standing wave; energy is stored in the oscillating loops.
Adjacent nodes are half a wavelength (λ/2) apart.
The Tacoma Narrows Bridge collapsed simply because the wind blew at its natural frequency.
Light damping hardly changes the period; it mainly reduces the amplitude over time.
items.answer: The Tacoma Narrows Bridge collapsed simply because the wind blew at its natural frequency.
items.markingKey: C. This is incorrect: The wind was steady, not periodic; the collapse is better explained by aeroelastic flutter, a self-exciting oscillation – a case where the textbook "resonance" story is an oversimplification.

items.stem: A student in Bogotá is checking notes on Faraday's and Lenz's laws of electromagnetic induction. Which statement is incorrect?
options: 230 V is the rms value; the peak voltage is 230√2 ≈ 325 V.
A strong magnet held still next to a coil induces a large current.
Maximum emf occurs when the plane of the coil is parallel to the field, where flux changes fastest.
Flux is zero then; it is greatest when the plane is perpendicular to the field (normal parallel to B).
items.answer: A strong magnet held still next to a coil induces a large current.
items.markingKey: B. This is incorrect: Induction requires a changing flux; a stationary magnet induces nothing, however strong.

items.stem: Which of the following best describes "flux linkage"?

The production of an emf in a conductor when the magnetic flux linking it changes
The direction of an induced current is such that it opposes the change in flux that produces it

items.stem: Which of the following statements about applications: radar speed measurement and astronomical motion is a common misconception? (Revision quiz set by Rafael.)

items.stem:
This question is about magnetic fields of wires, coils and solenoids.

(a) A student wants to test the relationship B = μ₀nI for a solenoid as the current I is varied. State which quantities should be plotted on the axes to obtain a straight-line graph, and state what the gradient represents. [3]

(b) Sana writes: "A longer solenoid with the same turns and current has a stronger field." Explain why this is inaccurate. [4]

(c) With the help of a specific example, explain why an iron core greatly increases the field of an electromagnet. [3]
items.answer: (a) Plot B (y-axis) against I (x-axis); gradient = μ₀n, from which μ₀ can be found. A non-zero intercept suggests a background field (e.g. Earth’s) or a probe zero error. (b) B = μ₀NI/L: spreading the same turns over a longer length reduces n and so reduces B. (c) The iron becomes magnetised: its magnetic domains align with the solenoid’s field and add their own field, multiplying the flux density many times. (A specific, correct example that illustrates this is required for full marks.)
items.markingKey: (a) [3 marks] Correct choice of axes: B against I (M1); straight line expected (R1); gradient = μ₀n, from which μ₀ can be found (A1). A non-zero intercept suggests a background field (e.g. Earth’s) or a probe zero error. (b) [4 marks] B = μ₀NI/L: spreading the same turns over a longer length reduces n and so reduces B. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation. (c) [3 marks] Award marks for: The iron becomes magnetised: its magnetic domains align with the solenoid’s field and add their own field, multiplying the flux density many times. (A specific, correct example that illustrates this is required for full marks.) (3 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem:
This question is about gravitational potential, potential energy and escape speed (HL).

(a) Why is gravitational potential always negative? [2]

(b) A projectile is launched vertically from Earth’s surface at 3000 m s⁻¹. Ignoring air resistance, determine the maximum distance from Earth’s centre that it reaches. [4]

(c) Distinguish between gravitational potential energy and gravitational potential. [4]
items.answer: (a) Zero is defined at infinity and work must be done to move a mass away to infinity (b) 6.86 × 10⁶ m (c) Potential (J kg⁻¹) is a property of a point in the field, V = −GM/r; potential energy (J) belongs to a mass at that point, Eₚ = mV = −GMm/r.
items.markingKey: (a) [2 marks] Zero is defined at infinity and work must be done to move a mass away to infinity (A1). V = −GM/r < 0 for all finite r. (b) [4 marks] ½v² − GM/R = −GM/r (M1); 1/r = 1/R − v²/(2GM) (M1); r = 6.86 × 10⁶ m (A1). (Less than escape speed 1.12 × 10⁴ m s⁻¹.) (c) [4 marks] Potential (J kg⁻¹) is a property of a point in the field, V = −GM/r; potential energy (J) belongs to a mass at that point, Eₚ = mV = −GMm/r. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

(a) A magnet is pushed into a coil connected to a meter. Which change gives a larger induced emf? [2]

(b) A student claims: "An emf is only induced if the circuit is complete." Identify the error in this claim and correct it. [4]

items.answer: (a) Alpha: helium nuclei, charge +2e, strongly ionising, stopped by paper/few cm of air; gamma: high-energy photons, uncharged, weakly ionising, reduced significantly only by several cm of lead or metres of concrete. (b) α and γ (c) Nuclear power contributes a tiny fraction (<0.1 %); radon, rocks, cosmic rays, food and medical uses dominate. (d) Measure background for 10 min. Measure counts over a fixed time at several distances d from a ruler mark, repeating each; subtract background. Since C = k/(d + e)², plot 1/√C against d: a straight line confirms the law and the x-intercept gives −e (the offset of the detection point). Use long counting times (N > 1000) to reduce the relative uncertainty (≈ 1/√N), handle the source with tongs, keep distance, minimise exposure time.

items.answer: (a) The minimum energy needed to remove an electron from the surface of a metal, Φ (b) The wave model treats light energy as continuous and spread over the wavefront, depending on intensity; the photon model treats light as quanta of energy hf, each absorbed by a single electron, so frequency determines whether emission occurs. (c) Eₖ,max = hf − Φ: doubling f more than doubles Eₖ,max because Φ is subtracted. (d) It is strong evidence for the photon (quantum) model of energy exchange, but light is best described by wave–particle duality.

items.stem:
This question is about spontaneous and neutron-induced fission; chain reactions.

(a) Explain why slow (thermal) neutrons are more effective than fast neutrons at causing fission of uranium-235. [3]

(b) A student claims: "The energy released in fission comes from the neutrons’ kinetic energy." Identify the error in this claim and correct it. [4]

(c) In one fission of uranium-235 by a neutron, the products are ¹³⁹Xe and ⁹⁵Sr plus some neutrons. Determine the number of neutrons released. [3]

(d) Fission of U-235 typically releases about 200 MeV per event. (i) Explain the origin of this energy using the binding-energy-per-nucleon curve (U-235 ≈ 7.6 MeV, fragments ≈ 8.5 MeV). (ii) Use these values to estimate the energy released. (iii) Account for the forms in which the energy appears and explain why not all of it can be used in a power station. [5]
items.answer: (a) The probability (cross-section) of absorption by U-235 is far greater for slow neutrons, which spend longer near the nucleus; fast neutrons tend to scatter or pass through. (b) It comes from the increase in binding energy (decrease in mass) as the heavy nucleus splits into more tightly bound fragments. (c) 2 (d) (i) Fragments are more tightly bound than uranium, so total binding energy increases; the increase equals the energy released. (ii) ≈ 235 × (8.5 − 7.6) ≈ 210 MeV. (iii) ~165 MeV kinetic energy of fragments, ~5 MeV neutrons, ~7 MeV prompt γ, plus delayed β and γ from fragment decay and ~10 MeV carried by antineutrinos that escape; the thermal energy is converted to electricity with ~33 % efficiency (second law of thermodynamics).

(b) [4 marks] It comes from the increase in binding energy (decrease in mass) as the heavy nucleus splits into more tightly bound fragments. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation. (c) [3 marks] Conservation of nucleon number: 236 = 139 + 95 + n (M1); n = 2 (A1). (d) [5 marks] Binding-energy argument (R1); estimate ≈ 200 MeV (M1 A1); forms of energy including neutrinos (R1); efficiency limitation (R1).

This question is about the nuclear model and Geiger-Marsden-Rutherford scattering.

(a) Explain the difference between the nuclear model and the plum-pudding model. [3]

(b) Estimate the minimum kinetic energy, in MeV, an alpha particle would need to reach the surface of a silver nucleus (Z = 47, A = 208), using R = R₀A^(1/3) with R₀ = 1.20 fm. [4]

items.answer: (a) A plot of stellar luminosity against surface temperature (decreasing to the right), on which stars fall into groups such as the main sequence, giants, supergiants and white dwarfs (b) Red dwarfs are small and dim, but red giants and supergiants are red (cool) and extremely luminous because they are huge. (c) 3.20 × 10¹⁰ m (45.9 R☉); red giant (d) It is a central organising tool that, combined with physical models, underpins our understanding of stellar evolution.
items.markingKey: (a) [2 marks] 1 mark for the core idea: a plot of stellar luminosity against surface temperature (decreasing to the right), on which stars fall into groups such as the main sequence, giants, supergiants and white dwarfs. (b) [4 marks] Red dwarfs are small and dim, but red giants and supergiants are red (cool) and extremely luminous because they are huge. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation. (c) [4 marks] L = 4πR²σT⁴ (M1); R = √(L/(4πσT⁴)) = 3.20 × 10¹⁰ m (A1); ≈ 45.9 R☉ → red giant (R1). (d) [5 marks] Arguments for: shows stellar groups and evolution; allows distances by spectroscopic parallax; cluster HR diagrams give ages (turn-off point). options: All matter has a de Broglie wavelength λ = h/p; diffraction has been observed for neutrons, atoms and even large molecules (C₆₀).
Λ = h/(mv): doubling v halves λ.
Photons always travel at c; the photon’s energy and frequency decrease, so its wavelength increases.
The Compton shift increases with the energy of the incident photon.
items.answer: The Compton shift increases with the energy of the incident photon.
items.markingKey: D. This is incorrect: Δλ = (h/mₑc)(1 − cos θ) depends only on angle; the fractional shift Δλ/λ is larger for higher-energy photons.

items.stem:
This question is about gravitational potential, potential energy and escape speed (HL).

(a) Why is gravitational potential always negative? [2]

(b) With the help of a specific example, explain why the Moon has no atmosphere while Earth does. [4]

(c) A student claims: "Escape speed depends on the mass of the rocket." Identify the error in this claim and correct it. [4]

(d) "Black holes are objects whose escape speed exceeds the speed of light, so Newtonian gravitation fully explains them." Discuss. [5]
items.answer: (a) Zero is defined at infinity and work must be done to move a mass away to infinity (b) The Moon’s escape speed (2.4 km s⁻¹) is low; at lunar day-side temperatures a significant fraction of gas molecules exceed it (or a sizeable fraction of the escape speed), so gas leaks away over geological time; Earth’s escape speed (11.2 km s⁻¹) is large enough to retain N₂ and O₂. (A specific, correct example that illustrates this is required for full marks.) (c) v_esc = √(2GM/R) does not depend on the escaping mass; a heavier rocket needs more energy, not more speed. (d) Newtonian reasoning gives the right radius but not the physics; general relativity is needed.
items.markingKey: (a) [2 marks] Zero is defined at infinity and work must be done to move a mass away to infinity (A1). V = −GM/r < 0 for all finite r. (b) [4 marks] Award marks for: The Moon’s escape speed (2.4 km s⁻¹) is low; at lunar day-side temperatures a significant fraction of gas molecules exceed it (or a sizeable fraction of the escape speed), so gas leaks away over geological time; Earth’s escape speed (11.2 km s⁻¹) is large enough to retain N₂ and O₂. (A specific, correct example that illustrates this is required for full marks.) (4 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.) (c) [4 marks] v_esc = √(2GM/R) does not depend on the escaping mass; a heavier rocket needs more energy, not more speed. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation. (d) [5 marks] Arguments for: setting √(2GM/R) = c gives the Schwarzschild radius R = 2GM/c², the correct result. Arguments against: the agreement is a coincidence: Newtonian theory allows light to rise and fall back, unlike an event horizon; general relativity predicts time dilation, horizons and singularities; models outside their domain can give right numbers for wrong reasons (NOS). Supported judgement: Newtonian reasoning gives the right radius but not the physics; general relativity is needed. Markbands (10 marks): Top band: focused, balanced argument, well-chosen specific evidence, and a reasoned judgement that follows from the analysis.

items.stem:
This question is about applications: radar speed measurement and astronomical motion.

(a) Which astronomical observation uses the Doppler effect to detect exoplanets? [2]

(b) Explain how the Doppler effect is used to detect exoplanets by the radial-velocity method. [4]

(c) Diego tested a radar speed gun by measuring the speed of a car driven past at a nominally constant speed several times. The 5 readings of the measured speed were 20.2, 20.6, 21.2, 20.8, 20.8 m s⁻¹. Determine the mean, the absolute uncertainty and the percentage uncertainty, and state the result to an appropriate number of significant figures. [4]

(d) Evaluate the use of the Doppler radial-velocity method for discovering Earth-like planets around Sun-like stars. [5]
items.answer: (a) Periodic shifts in the star’s spectral lines as it wobbles (b) A planet and its star orbit their common centre of mass; the star’s velocity along our line of sight oscillates, so its spectral lines shift periodically to red and blue; the period gives the orbital period and the amplitude gives the planet’s minimum mass. (c) 20.7 ± 0.5 m s⁻¹ (2.4 %) (d) Strengths: it measures the star’s line-of-sight wobble and gives the orbital period and minimum planet mass; it has found hundreds of planets. Limitations: an Earth-mass planet at 1 AU makes the Sun wobble by only ~0.1 m s⁻¹, requiring extreme spectrometer stability; stellar activity (spots, granulation) mimics signals; it gives only m sin i unless the inclination is known; long periods need years of data. Judgement: excellent for giant and close-in planets; for Earth analogues it needs combination with transit observations.
items.markingKey: (a) [2 marks] Periodic shifts in the star’s spectral lines as it wobbles (A1). Radial-velocity method. (b) [4 marks] Award marks for: A planet and its star orbit their common centre of mass; the star’s velocity along our line of sight oscillates, so its spectral lines shift periodically to red and blue; the period gives the orbital period and the amplitude gives the planet’s minimum mass. (4 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.) (c) [4 marks] Mean = 20.7 m s⁻¹ (A1); absolute uncertainty = half range = 0.5 m s⁻¹ (A1); percentage uncertainty = 0.5/20.7 × 100 = 2.4 % (A1). Result quoted to the same decimal place as the uncertainty. (d) [5 marks] States the principle (A1); strength with physics (R1); size of the effect quantified or explained (R1); two limitations (R1 R1); supported judgement (A1).
